dossier.summary: The paper studies, by simulation with exact finite-population GATEs on Stanford3, ego-Facebook, a BA graph and ER graphs, how accurate regression-adjustment GATE estimators are under exposure-based network interference. Its core findings (difference in means misses the spillover; the one-hop OLS is unbiased only under linear exposure response; misspecification bias is driven by extrapolation, does not shrink with n, grows with degree for a threshold response and changes sign with p; omitting the two-step exposure gives a predictable bias) are backed by 500-replication grids whose summary files reproduce the printed tables and almost all in-text numbers. The analytic first-order predictions (secant-vs-derivative cubic limit, 0.80*sqrt(d) threshold slope, two-hop projection identity) match the simulations closely, which supports the extrapolation explanation. Weaker points are a few overstated generalisations: the DiM bias equals the spillover only under Bernoulli and one-hop mechanisms, coverage under misspecification is not always near zero, graph-cluster randomization lowers variance under linear response, and the CR1 success relies on the shock partition being exactly the clustering used. The study does not examine multi-stage or mixed-probability designs, design-based estimators, or GNN regressors, so the task's question on reducing the bias is answered only through design choice (graph-cluster randomization) and alternative regressions. The record shows a single pre-specified simulation launch with no selection on evaluation results.

claims.quote: The difference in means and direct-effect regression estimate the direct effect and miss the GATE by exactly the spillover.
A one-hop regression is unbiased when interference is linear in exposure, but under nonlinear interference its bias comes from extrapolating to the all-treated and all-control exposures.
This bias does not vanish with sample size, and it changes sign with the treatment probability.
Omitting a two-hop term biases the estimate by a closed-form amount that our simulations confirm.
Heteroskedasticity-robust intervals undercover under community-level shocks, and cluster-robust intervals restore nominal coverage when enough clusters are treated.
Under misspecification, intervals have near-zero coverage and give no warning.
Second, the one-hop regression of \citet{chin2019} is a valid GATE estimator only when the exposure response is linear over the range that the GATE extrapolates to.
Graph-cluster randomization reduces some extrapolation bias but raises variance, and it can make a misspecified model look accurate by cancellation.
The threshold bias grows with $\sqrt d$, so denser networks make the naive regression worse, not better.
Gradient boosting was more accurate than the one-hop regression under the threshold mechanism, but less accurate under linear and smooth mechanisms at extreme $p$ and at high degree.
Precision scales with the square root of degree.
Clustering does not drive the bias.

issues.quote: CR1 is the natural estimator under GCR, where communities are the randomization units, and it also remains valid under Bernoulli randomization when the shocks are community-level (M6).
issues.why: In the code the M6 shocks are drawn on exactly the Louvain partition that CR1 clusters on (dgp.py simulate uses the same labels), so CR1 is given the true dependence structure; the abstract states the restoration of nominal coverage generally, and the paper does not say the clustering matches the shock structure by construction, which practitioners do not know.

issues.quote: The difference in means (DiM) has bias $-(\tau_m-1)$ in every mechanism, because the direct effect is 1 throughout.
issues.why: Under M4 the DiM bias is -2.97, -2.94 and -2.78 on Stanford3, ego-Facebook and BA (Tables 3-4), not -(4-1)=-3, because the two-step exposure f2 depends on the unit's own treatment; "in every mechanism" and "exactly" do not hold.

issues.quote: The difference in means and direct-effect regression estimate the direct effect and miss the GATE by exactly the spillover.
issues.why: The statement holds only under Bernoulli assignment; under graph-cluster randomization the DiM bias for M1 is -1.28 to -1.29 (Stanford3), -0.53 to -0.59 (ego-Facebook) and -1.11 (BA) in Table 4, not the spillover -2.

issues.quote: Under misspecification, intervals have near-zero coverage and give no warning.
issues.why: Several misspecified settings have CR1 coverage well above zero: ego-Facebook M2 B0.5 0.73, M3 B0.3/B0.5 0.55/0.58, M5 B0.3 0.63 (Table 4) and 0.74 for M2 at p=0.5 in E4; the paper concedes one such case in Section 5.3, so the abstract wording is too strong.

issues.quote: Heteroskedasticity-robust intervals undercover under community-level shocks, and cluster-robust intervals restore nominal coverage when enough clusters are treated.
issues.why: On ego-Facebook CR1 covers 0.91 (Bernoulli 0.5) and 0.92 (GCR 0.5) under M6; with 500 replications the Monte Carlo SE of a coverage near 0.95 is about 0.01, so these are below nominal, not restored.

issues.quote: In our graphs that cost is large under community shocks and small under linear responses.
issues.why: Table 5 shows graph-cluster randomization lowers, not raises, the one-hop SD under the linear mechanism (0.07 vs 0.11 at p=0.1, 0.04 vs 0.06 at p=0.5), so "raises variance" (introduction) does not hold for linear responses.

issues.quote: Gradient boosting on M1 is also inconsistent: its bias is $-1.03$, $-0.75$ and $-0.83$ at the three sample sizes.
issues.why: Inconsistency is inferred from three sample sizes with non-monotone bias and one untuned hyperparameter setting that is not scaled with n; the paper notes the fixed hyperparameters in its limitations.

issues.quote: These estimators are unbiased under the design but can have high variance when exposure conditions are rare, which is the situation at the extremes that the GATE requires.
issues.why: Design-based exposure-mapping estimators (Horvitz-Thompson/Hajek) are discussed but never run, so the practical recommendation compares the regression estimator only with difference in means and with other regression variants.

issues.quote: We estimated $b$ and $c$ by averaging 20 draws per graph (\texttt{code/diag\_omitted.py}).
issues.why: The slopes quoted mix rows of diag_omitted.csv from different treatment probabilities (Stanford3 b=0.036 and BA b=-0.001, c=0.148 are from p=0.1; ego-Facebook b=0.208 is from p=0.5), and the predicted biases gamma2(b+c-1) are not computed by any delivered script; the match to within 0.01 still holds with either row.

issues.quote: The number of replications (500) gives Monte Carlo standard errors for bias with median $0.006$ and maximum $0.13$ across settings (listed in the summary files)
issues.why: These figures are for E1 only; summary_E2.csv has Monte Carlo SEs up to 0.33 (two-hop OLS at degree 200) and E4 has median 0.015, and the checklist gives a lower end of 0.002 while the E1 minimum is 0.0008.

presentation.why: The main text cites script names and repository paths as evidence (code/diag_exposure.py, code/diag_omitted.py), and the Figure 4 caption points to summary_E3.csv for the M3 results.
The checklist template instruction block ("Delete this instruction block, but keep the section heading") was left in the printed paper.
In Figure 1 the legend box in the Stanford3 panel overlaps the difference-in-means markers for M3-M4; in Figure 2 the legend covers the M2-M3 region of the Stanford3 Bernoulli panel.
"SD 0.23 against 0.06" compares the two-hop estimator on Stanford3 with the one-hop estimator without saying so; a reader may think 0.06 is the two-hop SD on other graphs (it is 0.24 and 0.15 there).
No figure illustrates the exposure distribution and the extrapolation to exposures 0 and 1, which is the paper's central explanation; all figures are result plots.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: The total cost was about 3.6 hours of wall-clock time on a 4-CPU quota;
paper_mismatches.why: run_all.sh says "Runtime on 38 CPU workers was about 1 h in total" and launches 38 workers, which does not match the paper and README.

problems.why: run_sim.py, analyze.py, make_tables.py, diag scripts and run_all.sh hard-code /work/code, /work/results, /work/paper and /work/venv, while the delivery places code under code/code and results under code/results.
run_all.sh uses 38 workers and claims about 1 h, but the README and paper describe a 4-CPU quota and 3.6 h.

The raw ego-Facebook and Stanford3 archives and reps_E1.csv are left out of the delivery (archive/size); processed graphs and per-setting raw files are delivered, so summaries can be rebuilt but graphs cannot be rebuilt from raw ego-Facebook without re-downloading.

process_notes: All four experiments (E1-E4, 165 settings x 500 replications) were launched once at 09:52 as a detached run_all.sh (nohup) and finished about 13:33; the record sees only the 30-second launch, the outputs are the per-setting raw CSVs.
The analysis script was changed during the runs only to read partial per-setting files (steps 44-45); the failure at step 44 (empty concatenation) was fixed at step 45.

Late text checks against data (steps 106-113) corrected wording: a collinearity explanation was replaced by the measured Var(f2)/Var(f1), and exposure-dispersion numbers were added after writing diag_exposure.py.
Rework counted as the table regenerations at steps 93, 102, 104 (formatting of t_all_e1) and the figure regeneration at step 115 after the paper first used them; the values did not change.
The pdflatex build at step 97 returned exit code 1 from a trailing grep; the paper was built.

integrity.why: Estimators and GBM hyperparameters were fixed in code before any run (step 14); later comparisons of estimators are the reported findings, not a choice of a configuration by its score.

The only edits to evaluation code after runs began changed analyze.py to read per-setting raw files and to skip experiments with no files; metrics, truth and the experiment grid (defined before the single launch) were unchanged.
Simulation study: the estimators see only (z, f1, f2, x, y); the exact GATE is used only in analyze.py to compute bias and coverage.

Tables and figures are produced from summary files written by analyze.py on the detached run_all.sh output; the few hand-derived numbers (predicted two-hop biases, |z|<=2.2) trace to run outputs (diag_omitted run, step-106 check printing max |z| 2.22).
